sources.title: Human History Map, world-1600 historical-basemap topology
sources.note: Decoded locally with topojson-client. The 1600-1650 feature repeats the exact same Polygon and hash as 1530. It includes tested Udaipur, Kumbhalgarh, Jodhpur, Bikaner, Jaisalmer, Ajmer, Merta and Sirohi, but excludes Chittorgarh, Amber, Jaipur, Bundi, Kota, Dungarpur, Agra, Delhi, Ahmedabad, Gwalior and Multan.

sources.title: Tanuja Kothiyal, Scrambling for glory: assessing true Rajput identity in a Mughal war of succession, Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society
sources.note: Peer-reviewed article checked at lines 554-572. It describes coercion, conciliation, marriage and friendship in Mughal-Rajput alliance building; names Jodhpur, Bikaner, Mewar, Amer and Bundi as distinct pre-existing polities; and explains how imperial rank and revenue assignments could subordinate rulers while also strengthening their local kingship claims.

sources.title: IGNOU eGyanKosh, Unit 5: Mughal Conquest of Gujarat and Gujarat Sultanate
sources.note: University teaching unit checked at the section on Bahadur Shah and Humayun. It explains that Bahadur Shah attacked Chittor in 1534-35 because it could anchor expansion toward Ajmer, Nagaur and Ranthambore, and that Humayun then blocked his retreat and moved against Gujarat. It does not validate later rakhi legends.

sources.title: IGNOU eGyanKosh, History of Bharat, Unit 11: Rao Maldeo Rathore, Humayun, and Sher Shah Sur
sources.note: University teaching unit checked at section 11.3.2. It presents Rao Maldeo of Marwar as filling a political vacuum after Rana Sanga, describes his changing response to the exiled Humayun under pressure from Sher Shah, and places Marwar within the Humayun-Sur struggle rather than a united Rajput front.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Akbar I: Mughal India
sources.note: Scholarly encyclopedia entry checked at lines 41-48. It dates Akbar’s marriage alliance with Raja Bhar Mal of Amber to 1562, connects it with recruiting Rajputs into the bureaucracy, and records the 1568 capture of Chitor with a massacre of its garrison and the 1569 capture of Ranthambor.

sources.title: Pratyay Nath, Pilgrimage, performance, and peripatetic kingship: Akbar’s journeys to Ajmer and the formation of the Mughal Empire, Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society
sources.note: Peer-reviewed article checked at lines 615-628. It distinguishes alliance building with Amber, Bikaner and Jaisalmer from force at Chitor, Ranthambor and Haldighat; notes Man Singh’s 1576 victory without capturing Pratap; documents operations against Chandrasen; and explains Ajmer’s role in routes and campaigns.

sources.title: Victoria and Albert Museum, The arts of the Mughal Empire
sources.note: Museum essay checked for the travelling Mughal court, Persian administration and collaborative workshops, Jahangir’s long stay at Ajmer, and Nanha’s circa 1615-18 image of Prince Khurram receiving Rana Amar Singh’s submission. The painting is an imperial representation, not neutral documentary photography.

sources.title: G. N. Sharma, Mewar and the Mughal Emperors, IGNCA digital book
sources.note: Historical study checked around printed p. 117 and the chapter on the 1615 settlement. It cites an inscription dated 1588 for Pratap’s recovery and land grant, places his Chavand capital around 1585, and discusses the long Mewar war and settlement. Older readings are used with named evidence and not treated as infallible.

sources.title: Tanuja Kothiyal, Serving Empire, Building Kingdoms: Rajput State Formation and Political Culture in the Mughal Empire, UC eScholarship
sources.note: University dissertation record and abstract checked. It argues that Mughal expansion could cement Rajput political authority in agrarian hinterlands and lists Persian chronicles, Marwari and Malvi texts, land grants, inscriptions, court poetry, administrative records and built landscapes among its evidence. This supports a layered, not binary, view of service and sovereignty.

sources.title: Nandita Prasad Sahai, Politics of Patronage and Protest: The State, Society, and Artisans in Early Modern Rajasthan, Oxford Academic
sources.note: Oxford University Press abstract checked at lines 2522-2531. Based on petitions and legal disputes, the book studies the Marwar state’s relationships with artisans, caste hierarchy, coercion, concessions, customary expectations and resistance in rural and urban settings during 1500-1700.

sources.title: Sabita Singh, The Politics of Marriage in Medieval India: Gender and Alliance in Rajasthan, Oxford Academic
sources.note: Oxford University Press abstract and chapter list checked at lines 2526-2528. It treats marriage as political and social practice, connects matrimonial alliances to Rajput state formation, and explicitly analyzes sati, widowhood and jauhar in relation to women’s oppression rather than romanticizing them.

sources.title: NCERT, Themes in Indian History Part II, Peasants, Zamindars and the State
sources.note: Official textbook chapter checked at printed pp. 202-207. It uses seventeenth-century Rajasthan records for jati panchayats, petitions against taxes and unpaid labor, women’s complaints about husbands neglecting wives and children, and a Marwar manual in which Rajputs also appear as peasants. It warns that the Ain is a view from above.

sources.title: IIT Kanpur SATHEE, Peasants, Zamindars and the State
sources.note: IIT Kanpur educational transcription of the NCERT chapter checked for field and craft labor by women, cotton and oilseed production, the western Indian arrival of maize, tobacco’s spread and ineffective ban, village exchange, caste exclusions and collective petitions. General Mughal evidence is marked as regional context where not Rajasthan-specific.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Hill Forts of Rajasthan
sources.note: UNESCO property description checked at lines 39-49. It identifies forts as defended urban settlements containing courts, guards, homes, temples, production and trade, documents extensive water harvesting, and emphasizes varied terrain and an eclectic architectural exchange rather than one uniform Rajput style.

sources.title: UNESCO, Hill Forts of Rajasthan nomination dossier
sources.note: Nomination dossier checked at the Kumbhalgarh water-structures section around p. 113. It documents dependence on rain, planning of catchments, roughly ten dams and more than twenty baoris, outlet drains and Persian-wheel lifting. The dossier is detailed about water engineering but does not establish a typical household toilet for 1530-1650.

sources.title: ICOMOS evaluation, Hill Forts of Rajasthan nomination
sources.note: ICOMOS evaluation checked at the Amber Palace discussion. It describes Man Singh Mahal, 1589-1614, as a women’s residential court; servants’ quarters, stores and stables; privacy increasing through successive courtyards; and seventeenth-century water features and gardens. Later alterations are not silently assigned to Man Singh’s reign.

sources.title: Government of Rajasthan, Udaipur at a glance
sources.note: Official local-government page checked for the 1559 foundation of Udaipur, its setting by Lake Pichola and the oldest City Palace shrine. The page includes a hermit legend; the card separates that story from the dated urban foundation and does not repeat its romantic martial language.

sources.title: Government of India, Incredible India: Amber Fort
sources.note: Official tourism page checked for the conventional 1592 commission under Man Singh, sandstone construction, multiple courtyards and palace zones. Decorative features added later are not all backdated to 1592, and tourism superlatives are not used as historical proof.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Wonder of the Age: Master Painters of India, 1100-1900
sources.note: Metropolitan Museum catalogue checked at the Nasiruddin entry around pp. 98-100. It identifies the Chawand Ragamala as dated 10 April 1605, names its Muslim painter Nasiruddin, links it to Mewar’s court in exile and calls it a landmark in early Rajput painting.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Divine Pleasures: Painting from India’s Rajput Courts
sources.note: Metropolitan Museum catalogue checked at catalogue no. 6, p. 62. A 1605 Chawand Ragamala folio shows a prince, two women attendants, mirror, caged bird, bed, turban and white muslin jama. The catalogue transcribes its Devanagari label as desakararagini and translates the longer inscription.

sources.title: British Library Archives, IO San 3621: Mewar Ramayana folios
sources.note: British Library catalogue checked at lines 43-49. It records a Ramayana commissioned for Rana Jagat Singh, with its first book completed in 1649; surviving sections were written by Mahatma Hirananda and illustrated in several named styles, with other volumes completed after the atlas endpoint.

sources.title: Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts, Illustrated Ramayana Manuscripts
sources.note: Government arts centre overview checked at line 872. It identifies Udaipur as a prolific mid-seventeenth-century manuscript centre, describes bold outlines, vivid palettes and consecutive scenes in one frame, and notes that large illustrated manuscripts took years to complete.

sources.title: Tanuja Kothiyal, Sulh-i kull to Vedanta: The Dadu Panth and the Mughal-Rajput imperial paradigm, Modern Asian Studies
sources.note: Peer-reviewed article checked at lines 517-537. It traces Dadu Panthi networks with Amber and Marwar elites, merchants and Charans, the growth of vernacular Hindavi manuscript culture, and a circa 1610-20 hagiography, while resisting a simple court-versus-folk split.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, India xxxiii: Indo-Muslim Physicians
sources.note: Scholarly encyclopedia entry checked at lines 37-46 and 68-83. It documents sixteenth- and seventeenth-century Mughal court physicians, Persian works on Indian pharmacology, local drug substitutions, and intellectual exchange between Avicennian and Indian traditions. Court literature cannot establish ordinary access or effectiveness.

sources.title: British Museum, Top 10 historical board games: Pachisi
sources.note: Museum explainer checked for pachisi as an Indian cross-shaped race game documented from at least the sixteenth century, traditionally using cowrie-shell throws. It supports a period pastime in India, not a claim that every Rajput child owned a board or that elite and village play were identical.

sources.title: Victoria and Albert Museum, Indian textiles
sources.note: Museum essay checked for spinning, weaving, dyeing, woodblock printing and embroidery as specialized labor; the long-distance textile trade; and seventeenth-century court demand. It supplies Indian craft context, while the card avoids assigning every technique or surviving object specifically to Rajasthan.

sources.title: Ramya Sreenivasan, The Many Lives of a Rajput Queen, De Gruyter Brill
sources.note: University-press book description checked. It explains how gendered heroic narratives around Padmini changed while circulating among communities from the sixteenth through twentieth centuries and were later appropriated for political ends. It supports separating historical siege evidence from later memory.

proposedOverrides.name: Rajput states in the Mughal age: atlas umbrella
proposedOverrides.summary: Distinct Rajput states amid alliance, war and Mughal service, with forts, family life, work, writing, medicine, water and honest map limits.

batchIdentityNotes: Targeted only exact id rajputana: name Rajputana, approximate indexed map lifetime 1530-1650, kind state before review, and missing card before integration.

The exact target has two observed intervals, 1530-1600 and 1600-1650. Each is one single-ring Polygon with 11 coordinate positions, bbox approximately 68.8165,23.4542 to 75.7502,28.9448, and identical decoded geometry SHA-256 012eee7897344d6c48d15738cdb7e050224e99066c865ffcc98b615958fab2f2.

Named point tests put Udaipur, Kumbhalgarh, Jodhpur, Bikaner, Jaisalmer, Ajmer, Merta and Sirohi inside, while Chittorgarh, Amber, Jaipur, Bundi, Kota, Dungarpur, Agra, Delhi, Ahmedabad, Gwalior and Multan are outside.

In both snapshots, the target meets imported mughal-empire and islamic-and-hindu-states features. This is display topology and not proof of sovereignty, tribute, administration, cultural identity or a settled border.

The polygon cannot describe one government. The card separates Mewar, Marwar, Amber, Bikaner, Jaisalmer, Bundi and smaller domains, and distinguishes alliance, imperial service, coercion and resistance.
The 1530 and 1650 endpoints are imported map coverage. Neither is presented as the foundation or extinction of a Rajputana state.

Existing related cards and overrides for rajput-clans-and-small-states, rajput-kingdoms, hindu-kingdoms-1100, mughal-empire and other broad South Asian umbrellas were inspected. This bundle proposes no appliesTo and no additional override.
Public history claims are source-attributed. Gendered violence is described without romanticizing jauhar or sati; daily life and medical or sanitation claims state their evidence limits.
